\chapter{Tea and Milk, Two Roads}
\label{ch:te-tea-and-milk}
\hlchaptermodality{39}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can politely ask for tea or milk in Telugu, and say which word travelled by sea and which one three Dravidian cousins share under one regular sound law.}

Ask \te{దయచేసి} \te{టీ} and \te{దయచేసి} \te{పాలు}, follow \te{టీ} along its sea route through Hokkien and Malay against the overland chai route, then place \te{పాలు} beside Tamil and Malayalam's matching pāl against Kannada's own p-to-h shift.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[dayacēsi ṭī]{\te{దయచేసి} \te{టీ} (dayacēsi ṭī) — \textquotedblleft{}tea, please,\textquotedblright{} a word that sailed rather than walked}

\label{lesson:TE-C39-tii}



\begin{quote}
Two ways to say heart, done. \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} — please, taught earlier — is about to earn its keep again, in front of the drink you'd politely ask for first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{టీ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{టీ}} — \emph{ṭī} — \textbf{tea}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{దయచేసి} \te{టీ}.} — \emph{dayacēsi ṭī.} — \textquotedblleft{}Tea, please.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Day to day, Telugu politeness usually rides on the \textbf{-\te{అండి}} verb ending already named as the everyday carrier — but a bare request for a drink, with no verb at all, is exactly where \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} itself does the work instead.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{టీ}} is a direct loan from English \textbf{tea}. English's own word traces to \textbf{Hokkien} (Southern Min Chinese) \textbf{tê}, carried west by Dutch and English sea trade through \textbf{Malay} \emph{teh} and into Europe — the \textbf{sea} route.

That is the opposite road from the word most of Telugu's neighbours use. Hindi, Kannada, and Marathi all say some form of \textbf{chai}, which travelled \textbf{overland}: Mandarin \textbf{chá}, into Persian \textbf{\ar{چای}} (\emph{chāy}), and from Persian into North and South India alike. One drink, two Chinese dialects, two trade routes, two families of words — and Telugu's coastal contact with English trade left it holding the sea-word, \textbf{ṭī}, where its landlocked neighbours picked up the land-word instead.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dayacēsi ṭī\textquotedblright{} — tea, please
  \item the sea route — \textquotedblleft{}tê … teh … tea … ṭī\textquotedblright{}
  \item the land route it is not — \textquotedblleft{}chá … chāy … chai\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}tea, please.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Dayacēsi ṭī}.) Did \emph{ṭī} travel by land or by sea, and through which languages? (\textbf{By sea} — Hokkien \emph{tê}, Malay \emph{teh}, English \emph{tea}.) Which word, common in Hindi, Kannada, and Marathi, took the overland road instead, and through which languages? (\textbf{Chai} — Mandarin \emph{chá}, Persian \emph{chāy}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pālu]{\te{పాలు} (pālu) — \textquotedblleft{}milk,\textquotedblright{} where Kannada is the odd one out, not Telugu}

\label{lesson:TE-C39-paalu}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Ṭī} showed Telugu going its own way against most of its neighbours. This word shows the opposite: Telugu sits with the majority, and one cousin stands alone.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{పాలు}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{పాలు}} — \emph{pālu} — \textbf{milk}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{దయచేసి} \te{పాలు}.} — \emph{dayacēsi pālu.} — \textquotedblleft{}Milk, please.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{పాలు}} descends, unchanged, from Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*pāl} — matching Tamil \textbf{\ta{பால்}} (\emph{pāl}) and Malayalam \textbf{\ml{പാൽ}} (\emph{pāl}) exactly. Kannada alone says \textbf{\ka{ಹಾಲು}} (\emph{hālu}), because Kannada carries a \textbf{regular sound law} that turns a word-initial Dravidian \emph{p-} into \emph{h-}: the same law that turns Tamil \textbf{\ta{பத்து}} (\emph{pattu}, \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}) into Kannada \textbf{\ka{ಹತ್ತು}} (\emph{hattu}). Telugu, Tamil, and Malayalam all keep the original \emph{p-}; only Kannada shifted it.

So the pattern this chapter has been building — Telugu sometimes matching its neighbours, sometimes standing apart — flips one more time: here it is \textbf{Kannada} standing apart, not Telugu.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dayacēsi pālu\textquotedblright{} — milk, please
  \item the three that match — \textquotedblleft{}pālu … pāl … pāl\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one that shifted — \textquotedblleft{}pālu … hālu\textquotedblright{}
  \item tea, then milk — \textquotedblleft{}ṭī … pālu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}milk, please.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Dayacēsi pālu}.) Which three Dravidian languages keep the original \emph{p-} in \textquotedblleft{}milk,\textquotedblright{} and which one shifts it to \emph{h-}? (\textbf{Telugu, Tamil, and Malayalam} keep \emph{p-}; \textbf{Kannada} alone shifts to \emph{h-}, \emph{hālu}.) Name one other word pair that shows the same Kannada sound law. (\textbf{Tamil pattu, Kannada hattu} — \textquotedblleft{}ten.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṛ]{\te{◌ృ} — one character, met inside a word you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S131-vowel-sign-vocalic-r}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{థ} — what does it do? And one from further back: \te{జ}?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{◌ృ}}
\textbf{\te{◌ృ}} — \emph{ṛ}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{ṛ}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

This is the second shape of a vowel you already traced whole. Back at the seasons you met \textbf{\te{ఋ}}, the independent letter that opens \textbf{\te{ఋతువు}}. When the same vowel has to ride on a consonant instead of opening a word, it sheds that standing shape and becomes this mark. One vowel, two shapes, chosen by where in the word it falls — exactly the arrangement you know from \textbf{\te{ఉ}} and \textbf{\te{◌ు}}, and from \textbf{\te{ఎ}} and \textbf{\te{◌ె}}.

You already say this one:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{హృదయం}} \emph{hṛdayaṁ} — heart, the word for poems rather than for chests
\end{itemize}

Take it apart: \textbf{\te{హ}}, the letter from the borrowings, carrying \textbf{\te{◌ృ}}. Not \emph{ha} any more, and not \emph{hru} with a vowel added — the built-in \emph{a} has been swapped out, and what is left is \textbf{hṛ}.

\subsection*{Writing: \te{◌ృ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{◌ృ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two, and say which one carries the sign and which carries the standing letter
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{హృదయం}  ·  \te{ఋతువు}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{◌ృ} three times, saying \emph{ṛ} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} at \te{హృ}, and name its two pieces
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{◌ృ}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to, and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{ṛ} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Which standing letter is its partner? (\textbf{\te{ఋ}}.)

One more, from much earlier: \te{◌ీ} — what does it do?
\end{tcolorbox}
